# Renoxium: the developer documentation in one file

> Renoxium is a multi-tenant hosting platform for web applications and functions written in TypeScript. An app is TypeScript functions and HTML pages in folders that are its routes; it runs in a V8 isolate with its own SQLite file, under CPU, memory, wall-clock and network limits enforced by the platform, and it assembles auth, organisations, billing, admin, storage, email and other official modules instead of writing them. The toolkit a developer types is `renox`: the CLI (`renox new`, `dev`, `check`, `test`, `deploy`) and the npm package `renox` (types, helpers, test fakes).

The documents below are the developer-facing ones of https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/, in reading order, each introduced by a "Source:" line with its path and URL. Relative links inside a document are repository paths. The index is https://renoxium.com/llms.txt; the rendered pages are under https://renoxium.com/docs/.

---

Source: docs/07-app-model.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/07-app-model.md)

# 07 — Tenant application model

URL and behavior are determined by file location and name (convention over configuration). Configuration is only an escape hatch.

## Project structure

```
my-app/
├── renox.toml              app config + module list
├── public/                 static files, served by the gateway outside the tenant quota
├── pages/                  SSR
│   ├── _layouts/main.html  layouts (files starting with _ are not routes)
│   ├── _404.html
│   ├── index.html          /
│   └── products/
│       ├── index.html      /products
│       ├── index.ts
│       ├── [id].html       /products/:id
│       └── [id].ts
├── partials/               template components (<x-name>)
├── functions/              APIs: functions/api/checkout.ts -> /api/checkout
│   ├── ws/                 WebSocket handlers: functions/ws/chat/[room].ts -> /ws/chat/:room
│   ├── webhooks/           inbound webhooks (CSRF-exempt, signature-verified)
│   └── tools/              MCP tools exposed at /mcp (see 20-ai-agents-mcp.md)
├── migrations/             SQL owned by the app (tables prefixed app__)
├── policies/               Cedar policies owned by the app
├── jobs/                   scheduled jobs: jobs/nightly-report.ts with export const schedule
└── overrides/<module>/     override module templates without forking
```

## Routing rules

| Pattern | Example file | URL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static | `pages/about.html` | `/about` |
| Folder index | `pages/products/index.html` | `/products` |
| Parameter | `pages/products/[id].html` | `/products/42` → `params.id = "42"` |
| Catch-all | `pages/docs/[...slug].html` | `/docs/a/b` → `params.slug = ["a","b"]` |
| Not a route | `pages/_layouts/*`, `_404.html` | not directly reachable |
| API | `functions/api/orders.ts` exporting `GET`/`POST`/... | `/api/orders` |
| WebSocket | `functions/ws/chat/[room].ts` exporting `ws` | `/ws/chat/:room` |
| SSE | `functions/sse/orders.ts` exporting `sse` | `/sse/orders` |

Priority on conflict: static → parameter → catch-all. Ambiguous conflicts (two modules mounting the same path) are rejected at deploy time, not at request time.

## Pages: `.ts` and `.html` pairs are optional

| Files present | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `.html` only | Template rendered without loader data |
| `.ts` only | `load()` must return a `Response` (redirect, JSON, custom HTML) |
| `.ts` + `.html` | `load()` returns an object → template data |

The same rule applies inside `load()`: returning a `Response` skips the template; returning an object makes it template data.

```ts
// pages/products/[id].ts
import type { LoaderContext, ActionContext } from "renox";

export const guard = { action: "product.read" };

export async function load({ params, db, url }: LoaderContext) {
  const product = await db.queryOne("select * from shop__products where id = ?", [params.id]);
  if (!product) return new Response(null, { status: 404 });
  return { product, inStock: product.stock > 0 };
}

export const actions = {
  async addToCart({ form, db, session, authz }: ActionContext) {
    const productId = form.get("productId");
    await authz.require("cart.add", { id: productId });
    await db.execute("insert into shop__cart_items (session_id, product_id) values (?, ?)", [session.id, productId]);
    return { fragments: ["cart_badge", `product_${productId}`] };   // extra fragments rendered out-of-band
  },
};
```

Actions are invoked with `POST ?/addToCart`. They receive validated form data, run inside a transaction by default, and may return an object (template data for fragments), a `Response`, or `{ fragments: [...] }`.

**Why two files instead of a single-file component:** editors provide TypeScript highlighting and type checking without plugins, and the transpiler stays simple. A single-file format (`<script server>`) can be added later as sugar that is split at deploy time.

## Functions

```ts
// functions/api/orders.ts
import type { Handler } from "renox";

export const GET: Handler = async ({ db, auth, url }) => {
  const user = await auth.requireUser();
  const orders = await db.scoped({ user_id: user.id }).query("select * from shop__orders order by created_at desc limit 50");
  return Response.json(orders);
};

export const POST: Handler = async ({ req, db, auth, validate }) => {
  const body = await validate(req, OrderSchema);   // schema validation before the handler body
  // ...
  return Response.json(order, { status: 201 });
};
```

## Inbound webhooks

Webhooks from payment gateways (Stripe, Checkout.com, Telr, PayTabs, Network International), Apple App Store Server Notifications, Google Play RTDN, and similar providers are ordinary functions with platform helpers for verification, deduplication, and deferred processing.

```ts
// functions/webhooks/telr.ts  ->  POST https://<app>/webhooks/telr
export const POST = async ({ req, webhook, events }) => {
  const payload = await webhook.verify(req, { provider: "telr" });    // signature + replay check
  await events.emit("billing.payment_received", payload, { durable: true });
  return new Response("ok");                                             // respond fast; work happens later
};
```

| Concern | Platform behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Authenticity | `webhook.verify()` checks the provider's signature scheme (HMAC for Stripe, Checkout.com, Telr, PayTabs, N-Genius, JWS for Apple, Pub/Sub JWT for Google, or a generic HMAC/`secret` header for custom senders). Keys come from secrets. Failure returns 401 before user code runs |
| Replay / duplicates | Each verified event id is stored in `renox__webhook_events (provider, event_id, received_at)`; duplicates return 200 without re-emitting |
| Slow processing | Handlers should only verify and emit a durable event; the outbox worker does the real work with retries and dead-lettering (`10-modules.md`) |
| Direction and network rules | Inbound webhooks are not subject to the egress allowlist. Callbacks the app makes to the provider (receipt verification, status checks) need the host in `[permissions] network` |
| CSRF | Webhook routes under `functions/webhooks/` are exempt from CSRF tokens; they rely on signature verification instead |
| Rate limiting | Per-provider limits with a generous burst; verified events are never dropped by the limiter, unverified ones are |
| Local testing | `renox dev --tunnel` exposes a temporary public URL; `renox webhook replay <id>` re-delivers a stored event |

The `billing` module ships verified webhook handlers for Stripe, Checkout.com, Telr, PayTabs, N-Genius, and Tabby/Tamara, and adds Apple and Google subscription notifications in a later version (`18-build-plan.md`, M4).

## Scheduled jobs

```ts
// jobs/nightly-report.ts
export const schedule = "0 2 * * *";          // minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week
export const tz = "Asia/Dubai";                // optional IANA zone; UTC when absent
export async function run(ctx) {               // a named export (ops.md section 20)
  const { db, events, log, job } = ctx;        // job: { id, name, tick, attempt, payload }
  /* ... */
}
```

Jobs run as the principal `System::"app"` (a module's as `System::"<module>"`) with explicit permissions and are charged to the tenant quota. Each tick is one durable outbox row, run at least once and never twice at the same time; ticks missed while the tenant had no cell (an eviction, a restart, downtime) become one run for the latest of them. `ctx.jobs.enqueue(name, payload, { runAt })` queues a run of one of the caller's own jobs inside the current transaction. The `jobs` module shows the scheduled, queued, running and failed runs and retries or cancels them; `renox jobs` does the same for `renox dev`, which runs the scheduler only with `--jobs`.

## The `ctx` surface (SDK)

| Field | Available in | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `req`, `url`, `params`, `headers` | all handlers | Request data |
| `form` | actions | Parsed and CSRF-checked form data |
| `db` | all | SQLite bound to the tenant and the module's authorizer; `db.scoped()`, `db.transaction()`; optional Kysely/Drizzle drivers on top |
| `datasource(name)` | all | Handle to an external Postgres/MySQL declared in `renox.toml`, pooled in Rust (see `06-data.md`) |
| `kv` | all | Ephemeral in-memory cache per cell (not persisted) |
| `ai` | all | `chat()`, `embed()` against allowlisted providers or the platform AI gateway; metered (see `20-ai-agents-mcp.md`) |
| `webhook` | webhooks | `verify(req, { provider })`: signature check and replay protection |
| `domains` | all | `add()`, `status()`, `remove()` for domains owned by the app's own customers (see `05-tenant-lifecycle.md`) |
| `auth` | all | `requireUser()`, `currentUser()`, session helpers (from the auth module) |
| `authz` | all | `require(action, resource)`, `can()`, `canBatch()` |
| `session` | all | Server session (cookie-backed) |
| `events` | all | `emit(name, payload, { durable })` |
| `hooks` | services | `run(name, payload)` for modules that expose hook points |
| `realtime` | all | `publish(topic, payload)`, `subscribe(conn, topic)` |
| `secrets` | all | Frozen object of declared secrets |
| `config` | all | Module config from `renox.toml` |
| `render` | all | Render a partial to a string (for realtime payloads or email) |
| `fetch` | all | Allowlisted outbound HTTP |
| `log` | all | Structured logging (tenant-visible) |
| `deadline` | all | Remaining time budget |
| `offload` | all | Run CPU-heavy work in a separate pool with its own quota |

Types for `ctx`, `params`, services, events, and action names are generated into `.renox/types/` by `renox dev` (`12-developer-experience.md`).

## Configuration escape hatch

```toml
# renox.toml
[app]
name = "shop"
timezone = "Asia/Dubai"

[[routes]]
path = "/p/:id"
page = "products/[id]"     # legacy URL alias

[modules]
auth    = { version = "^1.0" }
billing = { version = "^1.2", mount = "/billing", config = { provider = "telr" } }
```

## State rules

Module contexts are reused across requests, so JavaScript globals are shared between users. Per-request data must go through `ctx`; globals are allowed only for intentionally shared caches. `renox dev` warns when a handler writes to global scope.

---

Source: docs/08-template-engine.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/08-template-engine.md)

# 08 — Template engine

Templates are valid HTML with logic expressed as attributes. At deploy time the attribute syntax is transpiled to minijinja source, compiled, and cached. At request time Rust only executes the compiled template. The syntax does not affect speed; the compiler and the data marshaling do.

```html
<r-layout use="main">
  <ul id="product-list" r-fragment="product_list">
    <li r-for="p in products" class="card" :class="{ 'card--empty': p.stock == 0 }">
      <a href="/products/{{ p.id }}">{{ p.name }}</a>
      <span r-if="p.stock == 0">Out of stock</span>
      <span r-else>{{ p.price | money }}</span>
      <button r-can="cart.add" :resource="p" hx-post="?/addToCart" hx-vals='{"productId": "{{ p.id }}"}'>Add</button>
    </li>
    <li r-empty="products">No products found</li>
  </ul>
</r-layout>
```

## Syntax

| Need | Syntax | Transpiles to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interpolation (auto-escaped) | `{{ user.name }}` | same |
| Filter | `{{ p.price \| money }}` | same |
| Raw HTML | `r-html="post.body"` | `{{ post.body \| safe }}` |
| Condition | `r-if`, `r-else-if`, `r-else` | `{% if %}` |
| Loop | `r-for="p in items"`, `r-for="(p, i) in items"` | `{% for %}` |
| Empty list | `r-empty="items"` | `{% else %}` inside `for` |
| Dynamic attribute | `:href="url"`, `:disabled="!ok"`, `:class="{ active: x }"` | attribute expressions |
| Fragment for partial render | `r-fragment="name"` | `{% block name %}` |
| Wrapper without output | `<r-group r-if="...">` | no element emitted |
| Component | `<x-product-card :product="p" compact>`, `<slot />`, `<slot name="actions" />` | macro, inlined at compile time |
| Component props | `<r-props product="Product" compact="bool = false" />` | validated at compile time |
| Layout | `<r-layout use="main">` | `{% extends %}` |
| Cross-module slot | `<r-slot name="admin.sidebar" />` | include from the slot registry |
| Permission | `r-can="action" :resource="x"`, `r-cannot` | `{% if can(...) %}` (see `11-authorization.md`) |
| Module component | `<billing:plan-badge :user="user" />` | namespaced macro |

`r-*` and `:*` attributes are removed from the output; `hx-*` and `x-*` are passed through. Interpolation uses `{{ }}` because single braces clash with `x-data="{ open: false }"` and `hx-vals='{...}'`; interpolation is not processed inside `<script>` and `<style>`.

## Right-to-left and bilingual output

Arabic is a first-class target (`21-uae-gcc-strategy.md`), so RTL is a template-engine requirement, not a theme concern:

- The layout sets `<html lang dir>` from the active locale; `dir="auto"` is emitted on user-generated text fields.
- Platform CSS and all official module templates use logical properties (`margin-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end`, `text-align: start`) and are snapshot-tested in both `ltr` and `rtl`.
- Built-in components (`<x-form>`, `<x-image>`, admin tables, pagination, date pickers) mirror correctly; icons that imply direction have RTL variants.
- Filters `money`, `date`, `number` follow the locale (AED formatting, Eastern Arabic digits optional, Hijri display optional); `t` resolves translations with Arabic plural categories.
- Bilingual documents (invoices, emails) are rendered from one template with side-by-side EN/AR blocks; PDF rendering uses fonts with Arabic shaping.

## Built-in components

Some components are provided by the platform or official modules and are compiled, not interpreted:

| Component | Provided by | Emits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<x-image :src="file" width="400" alt="...">` | `storage` module | `<img>` with `srcset` (1x/2x), `width`/`height` from stored metadata, `loading="lazy"`, `decoding="async"`, and URLs to the image pipeline (`06-data.md`, `18-build-plan.md` M6). Options: `fit="cover|contain"`, `focus="face|center"`, `placeholder="blur"`, `sizes="..."` |
| `<x-form action="addToCart">` | platform | `<form>` with the CSRF token, `hx-post`, and `hx-target` wired to the action's declared fragments |
| `<x-csrf />` | platform | Hidden CSRF input for hand-written forms |
| `<x-script src="...">` | platform | `<script>` with the per-request CSP nonce |

## The expression language is deliberately small

Property access, literals, comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `??`, and filters. No free function calls, assignment, or side effects. Logic that does not fit goes into the TypeScript loader. Because templates are a DSL with no code execution, tenant templates can be evaluated safely on Rust threads.

Filters are provided by the platform (`money`, `date`, `ago`, `number`, `truncate`, `json`, `upper`, `lower`) and by modules (declared in the manifest, implemented in Rust or as pure TS functions precomputed in the loader).

## Compile pipeline (deploy time)

1. Parse HTML with `html5ever`.
2. Resolve layouts, components, slots, and module overrides.
3. Validate: `r-else` without `r-if`, unknown components, bad props, invalid expressions, unknown actions in `r-can`, unknown fragments. Errors report file and line.
4. Emit minijinja source; let minijinja compile it. Consecutive static text becomes one chunk.
5. Record the fragment map (fragment name → block name → page) for htmx routing.

At request time the renderer executes the compiled template and writes into a single output buffer. No parsing on the request path.

## Where render time goes

For a 20–30 KB page with 100 items (estimates; must be measured, see `14-benchmarks.md`):

| Stage | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Parse and compile | 0 on the request path (deploy time) |
| Instruction execution | ~20–100 µs |
| Escaping (SIMD) + buffer writes | ~15–40 µs |
| **Marshaling loader data V8 → Rust** (`serde_v8`) | **~50–300 µs** |

The largest cost is not the engine but marshaling. Comparables: React `renderToString` 2–10 ms, Svelte SSR 0.5–2 ms, Hono JSX 0.3–1 ms.

## Two render paths, decided by benchmark (D7)

| | A. Render in Rust (minijinja) | B. Compile the template to a JS function, run in the isolate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Marshaling | Yes | No; data used directly |
| Execution | Rust interpreter over dynamic values | V8 JIT, fast once warm |
| Tenant CPU and heap | **Not charged** to the tenant quota | Charged |
| Safety | DSL evaluated by the platform | Same DSL, compiled by the platform |
| Wins when | Small to medium data, large pages, fragments | Very large data sets |

For multi-tenant hosting, path A has a non-technical advantage: rendering is done by the platform, the tenant isolate is free as soon as the loader returns, and the tenant heap stays small. Path B is kept for data-heavy pages. The default is chosen by the F2 benchmark.

## Optimizations and limits

- Static chunks are merged; a 500-node page becomes tens of instructions.
- Fragment requests render one block only, and the loader is told which fragment was requested so it can skip unneeded queries.
- Marshaling goes directly to `minijinja::Value`, without a JSON intermediate.
- Streaming: the `<head>` and layout shell are sent while the loader awaits the database.
- Fragment cache keyed by hash(data) + hash(user permission set); fragments containing resource-based `r-can` are never cached across users.
- Tenant templates can be a DoS vector (nested 10,000 × 10,000 loops on a Rust thread). Mandatory: minijinja `fuel`, iteration limit, output size limit, include depth limit, render timeout charged to the tenant quota.

## Secondary option: TSX

A loader may return JSX rendered inside the isolate. For teams that prefer the React style. It uses the tenant quota, so it is not the default.

---

Source: docs/09-htmx-realtime.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/09-htmx-realtime.md)

# 09 — Partial rendering and realtime

For partial page updates the server sends HTML fragments and the browser swaps only what changed. One template and one loader serve both full renders and fragments; no extra endpoints are written.

## Fragment flow

1. The first request to `/products` renders the full page.
2. htmx sends `GET /products?q=shoes` with `HX-Request: true` and `HX-Target: product-list`.
3. Rust runs the same loader (told which fragment is requested) and renders only the `product_list` block via minijinja's per-block render. The layout is not rendered.
4. The response is a few KB of HTML. htmx swaps the fragment with the `morph` extension (idiomorph), wrapped in a View Transition.

Actions that update several parts at once (a button and the cart badge) return `{ fragments: [...] }`; Rust renders the extra fragments and marks them with `hx-swap-oob="true"` automatically.

**Why it feels smooth:** morphing changes only differing nodes, so input focus, scroll position, playing media, and running CSS animations are preserved; the View Transitions API animates state changes between fragments. Elements with `view-transition-name` slide to their new positions.

## Interaction layers

| Need | Solution | Done by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First page | Full SSR | Rust + loader |
| Filter, paging, forms | Fragment + morph | Rust renders, htmx swaps |
| Dropdowns, modals, tabs | Alpine.js or vanilla JS | Browser, no server round trip |
| Highly interactive widgets | Islands (Preact/Svelte/Solid), bundled at deploy by the CLI | Browser |
| Notifications, feeds, progress | SSE | Rust |
| Chat, collaboration | WebSocket | Rust |

**Why htmx rather than a custom client:** htmx and idiomorph are mature and documented; the platform only needs to understand their headers on the server. A custom client is justified only later for tighter integration (automatic form validation from loader schemas, prefetching).

## Realtime: SSE and WebSocket

Connections are owned by Rust in the tenant's cell, not by the isolate. The isolate is invoked only on connect, incoming message, and disconnect, so thousands of idle connections use no tenant heap. Cost per connection is a few KB in tokio.

| | SSE | WebSocket |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Server → browser | Both |
| Good for | Notifications, feeds, progress, live fragment updates | Chat, collaboration, games, high-frequency input |
| htmx integration | `hx-ext="sse"`, `sse-connect`, `sse-swap` | `hx-ext="ws"`, `ws-connect`, `ws-send` |
| Through proxies/CDNs | Easy (plain HTTP) | Needs upgrade support |

```ts
// functions/ws/chat/[room].ts  ->  wss://host/ws/chat/:room
export const ws = {
  async open({ conn, params, auth, realtime }) {
    await auth.requireUser(conn.req);
    await realtime.subscribe(conn, `room:${params.room}`);      // checked by realtime.authorize
  },
  async message({ conn, data, params, realtime, render }) {
    const html = await render("partials/chat-message.html", { msg: data, user: conn.user });
    realtime.publish(`room:${params.room}`, html);              // HTML fragment to all subscribers
  },
  close({ conn }) { /* optional */ },
};
```

```html
<div hx-ext="sse" sse-connect="/sse/orders" sse-swap="order-updated">…</div>
```

- `realtime.publish(topic, payload)` can be called from WebSocket handlers, actions, services, or durable event handlers. Because all of a tenant's requests are on one node, pub/sub is in-process (`tokio::sync::broadcast`). Cross-node delivery exists only for replica-tier tenants, through a pluggable transport (NATS/Redis).
- Realtime from data changes uses SQLite's `update_hook`: changed table and rowid are mapped to topics and filtered by policy.
- Security and reliability (#118): an upgrade is refused with 403 before the hub or the isolate is touched when its `Origin` is not the app's own host (any scheme, same port) or one of `[security.cors] origins` exactly (`*` allows nothing here), when it is malformed or `null`, or when a WebSocket upgrade carries a cookie but no `Origin` (browsers always send one; a client with no cookie may omit it, and SSE may, since browsers omit it on a same-origin GET). `renox dev` rewrites its own origin to the app's. The principal is resolved from the session cookie once at connect and is `ctx.principal` in every handler. A topic is a Cedar resource: `subscribe` without a permitting policy is refused (fail closed), and a refusal in `open` closes the socket with 1008. Heartbeats; connection limits per tenant and per user; message size limits; backpressure (slow clients are disconnected, and one tenant's flood does not delay another's); SSE supports `Last-Event-ID` for short replay after reconnect. Tests: `crates/renox-realtime/tests/security.rs`, `crates/renox-cell/tests/realtime.rs`.
- Realtime is metered per tenant (connection-seconds and messages) for billing.

**Contract.** The runtime side of this section is `docs/contracts/ops.md` section 18 (1.5.0, #272): route kinds `ws` (`functions/ws/**`, `export const ws = { open, message, close }`) and `sse` (`functions/sse/**`, `export const sse = { open, close }`), the `conn` handle, `ctx.realtime` (`subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `publish`, `send`, `close`), payloads as text, JSON, or a partial rendered by the cell (`{ fragment, data }`, which is how the `render(...)` of the example above reaches subscribers), the change feed from `[realtime.feeds]` after commit, the `Origin` rule at the upgrade, the limits table (connections per tenant and per user, 64 KB messages, a 256-message queue with a 1008 close for slow consumers, heartbeats, `Last-Event-ID` replay), and one meter record per connection. The `realtime.authorize` hook named above is **a Cedar policy, not a hook**: subscribing is the action `realtime.subscribe` on the resource `Renox::Topic` (attributes `name` and `segments`), fail-closed when no policy permits it.

---

Source: docs/10-modules.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/10-modules.md)

# 10 — Module system and inter-module communication

A module is a mini app with the same folder structure as an app, processed by the same loader. Official modules (auth, org, 2fa, billing, admin, storage) are Renox's main product: the reason tenants choose the platform. The catalog and build order are in `18-build-plan.md`.

```
modules/billing/
├── module.toml     manifest
├── migrations/     SQL (SQLite dialect), tables billing__*
├── pages/  functions/  partials/  public/
├── policies/       default Cedar policies
├── services.ts     public contract for other modules
└── hooks.ts        event handlers, hooks, middleware
```

```toml
[module]
name = "billing"
version = "1.2.0"

[dependencies]
auth = "^1.0"
org  = "^1.0"

[config]
provider = { type = "enum", values = ["stripe", "checkout", "telr", "paytabs", "ngenius"] }
currency = { type = "string", default = "AED" }

[permissions]
network = ["api.stripe.com", "api.checkout.com", "secure.telr.com", "secure.paytabs.com", "api-gateway.ngenius-payments.com"]
tables  = "billing__*"
secrets = ["BILLING_PROVIDER_KEY"]

[exports]
views = ["billing__public_user_plans_v1"]

[[slots]]
name = "admin.sidebar"
template = "partials/admin-menu.html"
requires = "invoice.read"

[[tools]]                       # exposed through the app's MCP endpoint (see 20-ai-agents-mcp.md)
name = "create_invoice"
file = "tools/create-invoice.ts"
action = "invoice.create"
confirm = false
```

```toml
# renox.toml (tenant app)
[modules]
auth    = { version = "^1.0" }
org     = { version = "^1.0" }
billing = { version = "^1.2", mount = "/billing", config = { provider = "telr" } }
reports = { registry = "acme/reports", version = "^0.4", isolation = "isolate" }
```

At deploy: resolve versions and write `renox.lock`; build the dependency graph (cycles rejected); run migrations in topological order; merge routes under `mount` prefixes (conflicts rejected); register services, events, hooks, and slots with the Module Broker.

## Module isolation modes (D12)

| Mode | How it works | Call cost | For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `shared` (default) | All modules bundled into one context in the tenant's isolate | Plain JS function call, no serialization | The tenant's own modules and official modules |
| `context` | Separate context inside the tenant's isolate | Microseconds + serialization | Modules that need separate globals |
| `isolate` | Own isolate with its own heap limit, inside the tenant's sandboxed process | More expensive, cross-isolate | Marketplace modules |

Regardless of mode, table permissions are enforced by the SQLite authorizer and network permissions by the `fetch` op, never by JavaScript convention.

## Five communication mechanisms

| Mechanism | Nature | Needs declared dependency | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Service call | Synchronous | Yes | You need an answer now |
| Event | Asynchronous, fire-and-forget | No | Announcing that something happened |
| Hook | Synchronous, ordered, can halt the flow | No | Participating in another module's process |
| Public view | Read-only SQL, versioned | Yes | Joins across modules without N+1 |
| Slot | Template insertion | No | UI inside another module's page |

### Service call

```ts
// modules/billing/services.ts
export async function getActivePlan(ctx, userId: string): Promise<Plan | null> { /* ... */ }

// caller
import { billing } from "renox:modules";
const plan = await billing.getActivePlan(user.id);   // ctx is supplied by the broker
```

The broker checks that the caller declared the dependency, supplies the target module's `ctx` (db with that module's authorizer, its config, the same user, transaction, request id, and deadline), and generates `renox-modules.d.ts` for type checking.

### Event

```ts
// modules/billing/functions/webhook.ts
await ctx.events.emit("billing.invoice_paid", { userId, invoiceId, amount });

// modules/email/hooks.ts
export const on = {
  "billing.invoice_paid": async (ctx, e) => ctx.mail.send(e.userId, "invoice-paid", e),
};
```

| | In-process | Durable (default) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution | Immediately, in the same request | After commit, by the cell's outbox worker |
| Handler fails | Request fails | Retry with exponential backoff, then dead-letter |
| Server restarts | Event lost | Still delivered |
| Guarantee | Exactly once within the request | At-least-once; handlers are idempotent using `e.id` |

Durable events are rows in `renox__outbox` written in the same transaction as the data (D14). The outbox worker is woken by SQLite's `update_hook`, not by polling.

### Hook

```ts
// modules/auth/services.ts — auth EXPOSES a hook point
const result = await ctx.hooks.run("auth.after_login", { user });
if (result.halt) return result.response;

// modules/2fa/hooks.ts — 2fa FILLS it
export const hooks = {
  "auth.after_login": { priority: 10, async handle(ctx, { user }) {
    if (await isEnabled(ctx, user.id)) return { halt: true, response: ctx.redirect("/2fa/verify") };
  }},
};
```

### Public view

```sql
-- modules/billing/migrations/003_public_view_v1.sql
create view billing__public_user_plans_v1 as
  select user_id, plan_name, renews_at from billing__subscriptions where active = 1;
```

Modules that declare `billing` as a dependency may read this view (authorizer allows `SELECT`) and join it with their own tables. Internal tables stay private, so billing can change its schema as long as the view stays compatible. Views are versioned (`_v1`); the previous version is kept for at least one major release (D17).

### Slot

```html
<!-- modules/admin/pages/_layouts/admin.html -->
<nav><r-slot name="admin.sidebar" /></nav>
```

Slot contents are evaluated with the providing module's actions (`requires` in its manifest), so a menu entry disappears for users without access.

## Cross-module transactions

```ts
return ctx.db.transaction(async () => {
  const order   = await orders.create(cart);
  const invoice = await billing.createInvoice(user.id, order);
  await inventory.reserve(order.items);     // failure → order and invoice roll back
});
```

The broker uses the tenant's single writer connection for the whole transaction and passes it to every service call. This is the main advantage of the in-process architecture over microservices.

## Overrides and migrations

- Module templates can be overridden under `overrides/<module>/...`; logic cannot. The original file's hash is stored, and a diff is shown on upgrade.
- Migrations are forward-only with expand/contract (D17). Public views are versioned.

## Rules

1. Service calls and public views require explicit dependencies; cycles are rejected at deploy.
2. A module writes only to tables with its own prefix; other modules' data is reached through services, events, or views.
3. Event names, service signatures, hook names, slot names, views, and MCP tools are a module's public API, versioned with semver. `renox check` detects missing contracts.
4. Per-request data goes through `ctx`; module globals are shared across requests and may only hold intentional caches.

---

Source: docs/11-authorization.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/11-authorization.md)

# 11 — Authorization: RBAC, ABAC, and relations

There are two different kinds of permission. **Module permissions** (capabilities: what a module's code may do) are declared in `module.toml` and enforced by the sandbox, the SQLite authorizer, and Rust ops (`04-isolation-security.md`). **User permissions** (authorization: what an end user may do) are defined by the tenant application's policies and roles, and evaluated by one policy engine in Rust for all modules. This document covers the second kind.

| Model | Used for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RBAC | Most permissions, managed through the admin UI | Role `finance` may read and refund invoices |
| ABAC | Rules on user, resource, or context attributes | Refunds above 10,000,000 only by `finance_manager`; sensitive actions require 2FA |
| ReBAC | Ownership and membership | Document owner, organization member, team admin |

## Cedar (D15)

Policies are written in [Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com) and evaluated by `cedar-policy` behind a `PolicyEngine` trait. Native Rust, policies loaded at runtime, RBAC/ABAC/relations in one language, `forbid` wins over `permit`, and policies are validated against a schema at deploy time.

```toml
# modules/billing/module.toml
[authz]
actions   = ["invoice.read", "invoice.create", "invoice.refund"]
sensitive = ["invoice.refund"]                 # requires MFA, audit-logged
[authz.entities]
Invoice = { attrs = ["amount", "org", "status"] }   # only these fields are sent to the engine
[authz.default_roles]
finance = ["invoice.read", "invoice.refund"]
viewer  = ["invoice.read"]
```

```cedar
permit (principal in Role::"finance",
        action in [Action::"invoice.read", Action::"invoice.refund"],
        resource is Billing::Invoice)
when { resource.org == principal.org };

forbid (principal, action == Action::"invoice.refund", resource)
when { resource.amount > 10000000 } unless { principal in Role::"finance_manager" };

forbid (principal, action in Action::"sensitive", resource)
unless { context.mfa_verified };
```

Role assignments live in `renox__role_assignments (user_id, role, scope_type, scope_id)` in the tenant file, so a user can be `finance` in one organization and `viewer` in another. Templates and code always ask about **actions**, never roles; the role → action mapping exists only in policies.

Modules ship default policies under `modules/<module>/policies/`. The app adds policies under `policies/` and may override a module's under `overrides/<module>/policies/`.

**Contract.** The runtime side of this document is `docs/contracts/ops.md` section 17 (1.5.0, #272): the principal reaches Rust through the `auth` module's exported service `auth.principal` (never by the cell reading `auth__sessions`), cached per cell by session id and invalidated by `authz.roles_changed`, `auth.login`, and `auth.logout`; `op_authz_*` and `ctx.authz` (`require`, `can`, `canBatch`, `explain`, `roles`), the `guard` export, `db.scoped()` with `[authz.ownership]`, the append-only `renox__authz_audit` row for sensitive actions, and the evaluation count `authz_evals`. The Cedar schema qualifies the platform types this document writes bare: `Role::"finance"` is `Renox::Role::"finance"`, `Action::"invoice.read"` is `Renox::Action::"invoice.read"`, and a module's `Invoice` is `Billing::Invoice`. The `realtime.authorize` hook of the table below is a policy on `Renox::Topic`, not a hook (`docs/09-htmx-realtime.md`).

## Enforcement points

| Layer | How | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route | `export const guard = { action: "invoice.read" }` | Rejects before the handler runs; also applies to fragment requests |
| Action | `await ctx.authz.require("invoice.refund", invoiceFromDb)` | ABAC check with the resource loaded from the database, not from the client |
| Data | `db.scoped({ user_id })` + owner columns declared in the manifest | Replacement for RLS: ownership filter applied to every statement |
| UI | `r-can="invoice.refund" :resource="inv"` | Hides elements only; **not a safeguard** |
| Realtime | `Origin` check at upgrade; topics as Cedar resources, deny when no policy permits | Prevents cross-site sockets and subscribing to other users' topics |

Fail-closed rules (#118): every decision defaults to deny. No permitting policy, `forbid` matching, an unknown or anonymous principal, a missing entity or attribute, and an evaluation error each deny, and an error is logged with its reason (`authz_explain` shows it). A policy that does not validate against the merged schema (an unknown action or entity type) refuses `renox check` and the build (V24, V25), so it never reaches a cell. A realtime topic is a resource like any other: a subscribe no policy permits is refused. Tests: `crates/renox-authz/tests/fail_closed.rs`, `tests/schema_errors.rs`, `cli/tests/build-authz.test.ts`.

Example: the refund button is hidden because `inv.amount > 10,000,000`. The user still sends `POST ?/refund` with curl. The action calls `authz.require("invoice.refund", invoiceFromDb)` and Cedar denies with the same policy. Template and action cannot disagree because the source of truth is one.

## `db.scoped()` — the RLS replacement

```toml
[authz.ownership]
"shop__orders"     = { owner = "user_id", org = "org_id" }
"shop__cart_items" = { owner = "session_id" }
```

`db.scoped({ user_id, org_id })` rewrites statements against declared tables to add the ownership predicate (via SQLite's authorizer callback plus a statement rewriter for `SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE`). Official modules must use `scoped` for user-owned tables, and `renox check` flags unscoped access to tables with declared ownership. This is weaker than database-level RLS and is acknowledged as a trade-off (D16); authorization tests for official modules are mandatory.

## In templates

- `r-can` without a resource: O(1) lookup in the set of actions computed once per request. Cedar is not touched during rendering.
- `r-can` with a resource: one Cedar evaluation per item (microseconds), cached per (action, resource.id) within the request, counted as render fuel. Denied subtrees are not rendered at all.
- Alternative for large pages: `authz.canBatch("invoice.refund", invoices)` in the loader, then `r-if="inv.canRefund"`.
- Undeclared actions or attributes are compile errors at deploy. A resource missing a required attribute yields `deny` and a dev-mode warning.
- Fragment caches include the hash of the user's action set; fragments with resource-based `r-can` are never cached across users.
- Cross-module slots are evaluated with the providing module's actions (`requires` in the manifest).

## Cross-module context and audit

- Each module enforces policies for its own resources; the user identity travels with every service call.
- Event handlers, jobs, and cron run as `System::"<module>"` with explicit permissions, never as a superuser. Admin impersonation is recorded in the context and audit log.
- Decisions for `sensitive` actions are written append-only: who, action, resource, result, deciding policy.
- `renox authz explain --user alice --action invoice.refund --resource inv_123` prints the permitting or forbidding policies; `renox test` runs policy test cases (principal, action, resource, expected result) and per-role template snapshots.

## Performance

- Roles, memberships, and user attributes are loaded once per request and cached per cell; the cache is invalidated by pub/sub when roles or policies change.
- Policies are parsed and validated at deploy, not per request.
- Evaluation count per render counts toward the tenant's quota (together with render fuel), so a template with 10,000 `r-can` checks does not load the platform thread for free.

## Related security layers

| Area | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Authentication | `auth` module: phone-first (+971) OTP via WhatsApp/SMS, passkeys, argon2id passwords, OAuth/OIDC (Google, Apple, Microsoft), **UAE PASS** as an optional provider for resident identity, magic links; session cookies `HttpOnly` `Secure` `SameSite=Lax`; API keys/JWT for machines |
| 2FA | `2fa` module: TOTP and WebAuthn/passkeys via the `auth.after_login` hook and `context.mfa_verified` |
| Rate limiting | Per IP, user, and route at the gateway; strict on login and password reset |
| Input validation | Schema validation in actions and functions before the handler body |
| CSRF, headers | Tokens for all non-GET actions including htmx; CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` |
| Audit | Append-only for logins, role changes, sensitive actions, deploys, secret changes |

---

Source: docs/12-developer-experience.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/12-developer-experience.md)

# 12 — Developer experience

A tenant needs one CLI and an editor. Dev mode runs the same data plane as production locally, with SQLite, so laptop and server behave the same.

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `renox new <name>` | Project from a template (`shop`, `saas`, `blank`) |
| `renox dev` | Local server: hot reload, error overlay, type generation, local dashboard |
| `renox add <module>` | Add a module, update `renox.lock`, show requested permissions |
| `renox migrate` | Run migrations for all modules in dependency order |
| `renox check` | Type check TS, validate templates and policies, detect route conflicts and broken module contracts, lint unsafe SQL, scan for secrets (`--secrets`: only the secret scan) |
| `renox test` | Run TS tests in the production runtime, including policy test cases and per-role template snapshots |
| `renox deploy` | Bundle, upload, validate, activate; `--rollback <hash>` |
| `renox logs --follow` | Tenant logs |
| `renox authz explain` | Explain a policy decision |
| `renox db shell` / `renox db export` | Open the local SQLite file; export a tenant's file from production |

### `renox test`

`renox test [pattern] [--seed <file.sql>] [-u]` builds the app, adds a test-only service route to a copy of the artifact, and runs `bun test` with `renox/test` preloaded (#238). Each test file that calls `app()` gets the same prebuilt worker as `renox dev` (rule 5) on a fresh temporary tenant file: migrations applied, then `seeds/*.sql` and the `--seed` files. The helpers:

- `request`, `page`, `action`, each with its own cookie jar per user (`as(user)`), so session and CSRF work as in a browser;
- `service(module).<name>(...)`, through the broker like app code;
- a read-only `db` for assertions;
- `snapshot(html, { role })`, with request ids, nonces and CSRF tokens stripped;
- `installModule(name, source)` and `.upgrade(source)`, which return what `renox check` and the migration plan report;
- `policyCases()`, which reads `policies/tests/*.json` (`{ principal, action, resource, expected }`) as pending tests until Cedar is wired (F5).

Exit code 0 when every test passed, 2 when one failed.

### Installing the CLI

The CLI is released as standalone binaries (`bun build --compile`, so no Bun is needed) for Linux and macOS on x64 and arm64. A `cli-v<version>` tag runs `.github/workflows/release-cli.yml`, which publishes `renox-<version>-<os>-<arch>` with a `.sha256` for each binary, `install.sh`, and `worker-version.txt`. That file holds the `renox-worker` version the CLI is tested against: `WORKER_VERSION` in `cli/scripts/fetch-worker.ts`, whose release must exist before the CLI release. `curl -fsSL https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/releases/download/cli-v<version>/install.sh | sh` (source: `cli/scripts/install.sh`) installs into `~/.renox/bin`. It installs `renox` and the pinned `renox-worker` for the platform, and installs a file only when its SHA-256 matches. Override with `RENOX_VERSION`, `RENOX_INSTALL_DIR` and `RENOX_RELEASE_BASE`, or skip the worker with `RENOX_NO_WORKER=1`. `renox new`, `renox check`, and `renox build` of an app without `templates/` run without the worker; `renox dev` and the template transpile of `renox build` find the installed worker beside `renox`.

Releases are signed (#129; `docs/24-threat-model.md` F, "Tampered release"). Every `cli-v*` and `worker-v*` release also carries `SHA256SUMS`, a sigstore bundle `<asset>.sigstore.json` per file (cosign keyless signature from the release workflow's OIDC identity, logged in Rekor), and SLSA v1 build provenance (`renox-<version>.provenance.sigstore.json`, `renox-worker-<version>.provenance.sigstore.json`). The release workflow verifies all of them with cosign in a fresh container before it publishes. With `cosign` installed, `install.sh` also checks each file's signature and installs nothing that fails; `RENOX_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE=1` refuses to install without a verified signature. To verify a download by hand:

```sh
v=0.1.0; a=renox-$v-linux-x64
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS
cosign verify-blob --bundle $a.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/arif-rachim/renox\.rs/\.github/workflows/release-cli\.yml@refs/tags/cli-v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com $a
cosign verify-blob-attestation --bundle renox-$v.provenance.sigstore.json --new-bundle-format --type slsaprovenance1 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/arif-rachim/renox\.rs/\.github/workflows/release-cli\.yml@refs/tags/cli-v' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com $a
```

**The SDK** (`sdk/`, package `renox`, #376) is published to npm from the same `cli-v<version>` tag by `.github/workflows/release-sdk.yml`, at the CLI's version: `renox new` writes `"renox": "^<cli version>"`, so `bun add renox` (or `npm install renox`) in a new app installs the SDK that CLI was released with. The package holds compiled JavaScript and declarations (`dist/`, built by `tsc -p sdk/tsconfig.build.json`); `renox`, `renox/kysely`, `renox/drizzle`, `renox/fakes` and `renox/test` are its entry points. It is published with npm provenance (`npm publish --provenance`, the OIDC identity of the release workflow, logged in Sigstore): `npm view renox --json | jq .dist.attestations` shows it, and `npm audit signatures` checks it in an app. The workflow refuses a tag whose version differs from `sdk/package.json` or `cli/package.json`, and a pull request that changes `sdk/` or the workflow runs the build, the packed-package test (`sdk/tests/pack.test.ts`) and `npm publish --dry-run --provenance` without publishing.

For a worker use `release-worker\.yml@refs/tags/worker-v` and the worker release's files. The CLI checks the worker before it runs it: the downloaded or installed worker must have the sha256 of the pinned release for its platform, baked into the CLI (`PINNED_WORKER` in `cli/src/worker/verify.ts`, checked against the worker release when the CLI is released); `renox dev --worker <path>` also accepts a binary whose `<path>.sigstore.json` and the release's provenance bundle beside it verify with cosign as above. Anything else stops with `RENOX_CLI_WORKER_UNVERIFIED` (exit code 3) and the expected and actual sha256. `RENOX_WORKER_PATH` is the unverified override for a worker built from source.

## Build with an AI agent

The platform is built to be driven by a coding agent as well as by a person (`docs/20-ai-agents-mcp.md`; #377). What an agent gets, and the rules it works under:

**In every new app.** `renox new` writes three files next to `renox.toml` (`cli/templates/`): `AGENTS.md` (the app model in short: folders are routes; the commands; the rules agents break most: parameterised SQL, no module-level state, `fetch` hosts and secret names declared in `renox.toml`, `guard` exports for authorization; where the docs for models are), `CLAUDE.md` ("Read `AGENTS.md` first"), and `.mcp.json`, which registers the local MCP server:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "renox": { "command": "renox", "args": ["mcp", "--project", "."] } } }
```

Claude Code reads `.mcp.json` as is. Cursor reads the same object from `.cursor/mcp.json`; Codex and other clients that take a stdio MCP server take the same command. `renox mcp` (`cli/README.md`, "`renox mcp`") serves `dev_status`, `dev_errors` (what the error overlay shows), `run_check`, `run_tests`, `search_docs`, `authz_explain`, `list_policies`, `list_tools`, `list_agent_tokens` and `revoke_agent_token`, and the resources `docs://`, `types://renox/ctx.d.ts`, `config://effective`, `routes://` and `policies://`. Every tool is one fixed operation on the project folder: model input never becomes a shell command or a path, and `.env` values are redacted from every result. The documentation for models is at <https://renoxium.com/llms.txt> (the index) and <https://renoxium.com/llms-full.txt> (the developer documents in one file), generated from this repository (`www/scripts/llms.ts`).

**The remote platform MCP** (`mcp.renoxium.com`, `control/api/src/mcp/README.md`) is for agents that are not on the developer's machine: `list_apps`, `get_app`, `create_app`, `list_deployments`, `get_deployment`, `activate`, `rollback`, `get_logs`, `list_secrets` (names only, never a value), `get_usage`. It is behind OAuth 2.1 with PKCE; a token is a tenant token named `mcp: <client>` that lives one hour, holds at most the signed-in user's role, and carries the scopes `apps:read`, `apps:write`, `deploy`, `logs:read`, `secrets:read` (each optionally narrowed to one app; `secrets:write` and `tokens:write` are never granted to an agent). The default grant is `apps:read logs:read secrets:read deploy`. Mutating tools (`create_app`, `activate`, `rollback`) do nothing on the first call: they return a plan and a confirmation token bound to the exact arguments, and run on the second call with it, once. Log lines come back marked `untrusted: true`. The dashboard and `renox tokens list` show and revoke these tokens like any other.

**App MCP.** An app is itself an MCP server at `/mcp`: every `functions/tools/*.ts` and every tool a module declares is listed, authenticated by the `auth` module's OAuth server, authorized by the tool's Cedar `action` exactly like a button in the UI, rate-limited and metered to the tenant; a tool with `confirm: true` returns a preview first (`docs/20`, section 2).

**In-app agents.** Tenant code calls models with `ctx.ai.chat(...)` (`ops.md`, `op_ai_chat`): the provider host must be in `[permissions] network`, the key in a declared secret, or the request goes through the platform's AI gateway; tokens count toward the tenant's limits, and local tools run in the same isolate under the same authorization (`docs/20`, section 3).

**What an agent may and may not do** (`docs/20`, section 5): results that come from the database, logs or user content are data, labelled `untrusted: true`, never instructions; destructive operations (`rollback`, `activate`, `revoke_agent_token`, `db_execute`) need the confirmation step, and the local server shows the confirmation to the person in the terminal; a module's permission diff (`renox add`) is shown, never auto-approved; secrets are never serialized through MCP (names and versions only) and are redacted from logs and errors; every call is audited with the actor `agent`, the client and, when reported, the model; tokens are short-lived and listed in the dashboard, where a tenant revokes them.

## Dev loop

1. A file watcher detects a change.
2. Only the changed file is processed: TS transpiled (swc), templates transpiled to minijinja and recompiled.
3. The isolate is discarded and recreated from the snapshot (D19). SQLite connections stay open.
4. The browser is refreshed via SSE; if only a template changed, only the fragment is swapped.

Target from save to browser update: under 300 ms for a single file. Discarding the isolate costs tens of milliseconds and removes the memory-leak risk of hot-swapping contexts.

## Type safety

`renox dev` generates `.renox/types/`: `LoaderContext`, `params` per route (from file names), each module's services, event payloads, policy action names, and fragment names. Type checking happens in the editor through `tsc`/tsgo; the runtime does not type check so reloads stay fast.

## Debugging

- TS → JS source maps ship in the bundle and are mapped by the Deno runtime, so stack traces point at the original TS lines.
- Errors from Rust ops (query, fetch, render) are wrapped as JS errors with context (table name, host, template name and line).
- In dev, elements hidden by `r-can` are shown as placeholders with the name of the deciding policy.
- `renox dev --inspect` exposes the V8 inspector for breakpoints in VS Code.

## Client-side errors

Server errors alone are not enough: an exception in an Alpine component or an island, an htmx fragment that returned an error or found no swap target, or a script blocked by the CSP would otherwise leave a page that "does nothing". The platform captures these from the browser (`docs/contracts/client-events.md`, #125):

- Every response carries `x-renox-request-id` (the gateway sets it on every response, its own 400, 431, 429, and 503 included). Pages also carry it in `<meta name="renox-request-id">`, with `<meta name="renox-deployment">` and, on error pages, `<meta name="renox-error-code">`; fragments carry it in the header only (contract section 1). A browser error is reported with the id of the page or fragment on screen, so the overlay shows the server log and the browser error of the same request on one screen.
- The platform script `/__renox/client.js` (`sdk/client/`, about 2.5 KB gzipped, CI fails above 4 KB) is the first thing in every page's `<head>`, with the request's CSP nonce. It captures `window` errors (message, file, line, column, stack frames), unhandled rejections, `htmx:responseError` (status and the `RENOX_*` code from the JSON body or the error page's meta tag, with the failed request's own id), `htmx:sendError`, `htmx:timeout`, `htmx:targetError`, `htmx:swapError`, and `securitypolicyviolation`. Identical events within 10 s are sent once, at most 50 per page load, in batches of up to 20 to `/__renox/events` with `sendBeacon` (fetch `keepalive` as fallback), at the latest one second after the first event or when the page is hidden. `<meta name="renox-events-sample" content="0.1">` keeps one page load in ten. Realtime events (`renox.realtime.connect()`) come with F5 (#70).
- **`renox:error` hook.** Every captured event is also dispatched on `document` as a `renox:error` DOM event whose `detail` is the event as sent, so the app can show its own toast: `document.addEventListener("renox:error", (e) => toast(e.detail.kind))`. `renox.client.setExtra({ plan: "pro" })` adds up to 16 tenant fields (1 KB) to later events.
- The gateway validates and rate-limits the events per IP and per tenant before writing them to the tenant log sink with `source=client`; the endpoint never touches the isolate and always answers 204. The endpoint, batch format, and limits (32 KB body, 20 events, 60 requests per minute per IP, 1,000 events per minute per tenant then sampled, a daily cap) are in `docs/contracts/client-events.md` sections 2, 3, and 7. CSP reports from the browser itself (`report-uri`, `report-to renox-csp`) go to the same endpoint.
- **In dev** (`renox dev`): the proxy marks every page with `<meta name="renox-dev">`, which also turns on `console.error` capture, and handles the batches itself, so nothing is dropped or sampled. Each event is printed in the terminal next to the server lines, for example `[browser] js.error pages/products/[id].html:42:7 TypeError: cart is undefined (01JBQ3Z7MA…)` (an inline script's errors name the page's template; the line is the line in the served HTML), and an event with a `RENOX_*` code gets the catalogue's hint. The overlay's "Browser" tab lists the events with source, line, column, stack, and request id; "Server log for <id>" shows the server side of that request (code, limit, cpu_ms, heap) in the same panel. The MCP `dev_errors` tool returns them as `browserErrors` (`kind`, `message`, `request_id`, `url`, `code`, `detail`). The events are kept in `.renox/logs/browser.ndjson`.
- In production the dashboard groups events by fingerprint per deployment, flags regressions, and symbolicates frames against sourcemaps that `renox deploy` uploads privately (never served) (#128).
- Privacy: no cookies, form values, or storage are read; URLs other than the page's lose their query and fragment; stack frames keep file, line, column, and function only (`docs/contracts/client-events.md` section 8). `[client] events = false` in `renox.toml` is to disable the script and the endpoint once the manifest carries it (contract Open 1; the worker already reads `client.events`).

## Deploy without downtime

1. `renox deploy` produces an artifact with a content hash.
2. The control plane validates it and runs migrations (forward-only, so the old deployment keeps working during the switch).
3. The new isolate is prepared alongside the old one.
4. The route pointer is switched atomically; in-flight requests finish on the old version.
5. Rollback is a pointer switch to the previous hash.

## Concurrency and the blast radius

A quiet deployment runs in one isolate. When requests start waiting on a busy isolate, the worker grows a pool of isolates for that deployment (up to 2 on the free tier, up to one per core and at most 8 on paid tiers), keeps one spare ready, and sends each request to the least-loaded isolate (#156). A request that hits the CPU or heap limit ends its own isolate and every request in flight on that isolate, which get the same 503 code; requests on the other isolates of the pool carry on, and the spare takes the dead isolate's place. Module-level state (in-memory caches, counters) lives per isolate, so two requests of one deployment can see different copies: keep shared state in `ctx.db`. The concurrency limit (50 free, 500 paid) counts the requests of the whole pool.

## Build and compile strategy (for platform developers)

Two different people compile things, and the experience must differ.

| Who | Writes | Compiles | Expected feedback loop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant developer | TypeScript, HTML, SQL | Nothing. TS is transpiled (types stripped) in milliseconds; templates are re-transpiled in milliseconds | Save → browser in ≤ 300 ms; `renox test` runs hundreds of TS tests in seconds inside the prebuilt runtime |
| Platform developer (us) | Rust data plane, plus TypeScript control plane, CLI, SDK, modules | Rust only for the data plane; everything else is Bun with no build step | `cargo check` in seconds for a leaf crate; full release build only in CI when Rust changes |

Tenants never touch Rust. The pain of Rust compile times is confined to the data plane, and the rules below keep it small.

### Rules

1. **Never compile V8.** Use prebuilt `rusty_v8` binaries (the default of the `v8` crate). V8 from source is 30–60 minutes and is never part of our build. Pin the version.
2. **Small crates, strict boundaries.** `renox-data`, `renox-template`, `renox-authz`, `renox-realtime`, `renox-meter`, `renox-gateway` are leaf crates that do not depend on the runtime or on each other. Editing the template engine recompiles only that crate. Integration happens only in `renox-cell`.
3. **Fast linking and incremental builds.** `mold` (Linux) or `lld` as the linker; `cargo watch -x check` during iteration; `opt-level = 1` for dependencies in the dev profile; `debug = 1` to cut debuginfo size.
4. **Tests without V8 wherever possible.** The template engine is tested as string in → string out; the authorizer and migrations against a real SQLite file; Cedar policies against policy files; the gateway with in-memory requests. Only `renox-runtime` and `renox-cell` link V8, and their tests run less often (CI and on demand).
5. **Dev-mode runtime is prebuilt.** `renox dev` ships the compiled worker, so the tenant feedback loop never includes a Rust build. The same prebuilt worker is used for `renox test`.
6. **CI caches everything.** `sccache` + cached `target/`; the release build of `renox-worker` runs only when `crates/` changes. Docs, TypeScript, and module changes never trigger a Rust build. Target: CI ≤ 15 minutes with a warm cache (B20).
   **CI minutes (#189).** Every check sits in one of three jobs: `lint` (path filter, pinned actions, `cargo-deny`, `bun audit`, and the docs checks when docs change) runs on every push and PR, `rust` and `ts` only when their paths change, so a docs-only PR bills one job. On a pull request `rust` tests only the crates that changed and the workspace packages that depend on them (`make rust-test CRATES=...`); a change outside `crates/` (lockfile, toolchain, `ops/`, the workflow) tests the whole workspace, and so does every push to `main`. `release-worker.yml` runs on `worker-v*` tags, by hand, and once on `main` after a merge that touches the packaging, never on a pull request. Quota decision, taken by the owner on 2026-10-28 when 1,800 of the plan's 2,000 monthly minutes were used: option (c), the repository is public, so standard GitHub-hosted runners are not metered. Rejected: (a) a paid spending limit for overage (USD 0.008 a Linux minute), kept as the fallback if the repository ever goes private again; (b) a self-hosted runner for `rust` on the owner's build machine, which on a public repository would run code from fork pull requests on that machine. The job folding stays because it shortens the PR feedback loop and the concurrency queue.
7. **Most of the platform is not Rust.** Control plane, CLI, SDK, and all official modules are TypeScript on Bun. Expected split of code we write: roughly 30–40% Rust (data plane glue over Supabase Edge Runtime), 60–70% TypeScript.
8. **`unsafe` and FFI stay in two places.** V8 and SQLite wrappers only, documented and reviewed. This keeps compile-heavy, hard-to-test code isolated.

### Expected numbers (targets, measured under B20)

| Build | Cold | Warm (one leaf crate changed) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cargo check` workspace | ≤ 3 min | ≤ 5 s |
| `cargo build` debug (with V8 prebuilt) | ≤ 6 min | ≤ 20 s |
| `cargo test` leaf crates (no V8) | ≤ 1 min | ≤ 10 s |
| `cargo build --release renox-worker` (CI) | ≤ 15 min with cache | — |

If these targets are missed, the fix is more crate splitting or moving logic out of the V8-linked crates, not accepting slower loops.

## Observability

OpenTelemetry tracing per request: spans for the loader, each service call, query, render, and outbound fetch. Metrics per tenant and per route: latency, error rate, CPU ms, heap, egress. Structured logs always include `tenant_id`, `request_id`, and module name. Tenants see their own traces and metrics in the dashboard.

---

Source: docs/20-ai-agents-mcp.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/20-ai-agents-mcp.md)

# 20 — AI agents and MCP

AI agents touch Renox at three points, each with its own mechanism and trust boundary. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the integration surface for the first two; the third is tenant code calling model providers.

| Entry point | Who the agent is | Talks to | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Platform MCP | A developer's Claude Code / Cursor / Codex | The Renox control plane and the local dev server | "Deploy this app, show the last errors, why was this refund denied?" |
| 2. App MCP | An end user's agent (Claude, ChatGPT, a custom agent) | A tenant application | "Create an invoice for PT Maju, check stock for shoe size 42" |
| 3. In-app agents | Tenant code | Model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, local) | A support chatbot in a shop, report summaries |

A fourth, non-protocol surface is the repository itself: `AGENTS.md`, `docs/`, and agent-friendly CLI output.

## 1. Platform MCP: Renox as an MCP server for developers

```
renox mcp            # local, stdio transport; for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex
mcp.renoxium.com     # remote, Streamable HTTP + OAuth 2.1; for cloud agents
```

### Tools

All results are structured JSON with the same error shapes as the CLI (`file`, `line`, `code`, `hint`), so an agent can fix problems without parsing prose.

| Group | Tools | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apps and deploys | `list_apps`, `create_app`, `deploy`, `rollback`, `get_deployment`, `list_deployments` | `deploy` returns the validation report (templates, policies, routes, permissions) |
| Observability | `get_logs(filter, since, limit)`, `get_metrics(range)`, `get_trace(request_id)` | Logs are truncated and secret-redacted |
| Data | `db_schema`, `db_query(sql)` (read-only by default), `db_execute(sql)` (write scope + confirmation), `db_export` | Same authorizer; row and time limits |
| Modules | `search_registry`, `add_module`, `module_permissions_diff`, `upgrade_module`, `list_module_contracts` | Permission diffs are returned to the agent, never auto-approved |
| Security | `authz_explain(user, action, resource)`, `security_check` | JSON form of `renox check --security` |
| Local dev | `dev_status`, `dev_errors`, `run_check`, `run_tests`, `generate_types` | The agent sees the same error overlay a human sees in the browser |
| Docs | `search_docs(query)` | Full-text search over this documentation and module READMEs |
| Authorization (local, #294) | `authz_explain(user, action, resource?, roles?)`, `list_policies` | Read-only. The deciding policies with their text; the merged set's files, actions, entities and default roles |
| App MCP (local, #294) | `list_tools`, `list_agent_tokens`, `revoke_agent_token(id, confirm)` | The app's tools from a build; the dev app's agent tokens. Revoking is destructive: `confirm` repeats the id |

### Resources

`docs://` (this documentation), `config://effective` (resolved `renox.toml`), `routes://`, `schema://db`, `types://generated`, `modules://permissions`, `module://<name>/readme`.

### Prompts

Task templates with the right context preloaded: `add-module`, `debug-failing-deploy`, `write-migration`, `explain-denied-action`, `optimize-slow-route`.

### Security of the platform MCP

- OAuth 2.1 tokens with **per-tool scopes**: `apps:read`, `apps:write`, `deploy:write`, `logs:read`, `db:read`, `db:write`, `modules:write`, `secrets:none` (secrets are never readable through MCP; only names and versions). Default grant for an agent: read scopes + `deploy:write`.
- Destructive tools (`rollback`, `db_execute`, `delete_app`, `upgrade_module`) return a **plan plus a confirmation token**; execution requires a second call with that token. In the local stdio server, the confirmation is shown to the human in the terminal.
- Every call is audit-logged with actor type `agent`, the client name, and the model if reported.
- Tokens are short-lived; the local server inherits the developer's CLI login.

## 2. App MCP: every tenant application can be an MCP server

Tenants do not write MCP servers. They declare tools, and the platform exposes `/mcp` for the app with authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and metering already applied.

```ts
// functions/tools/create-invoice.ts
import { tool } from "renox";
import { z } from "zod";

export default tool({
  name: "create_invoice",
  description: "Create a draft invoice for a customer",
  input: z.object({
    customerId: z.string(),
    items: z.array(z.object({ sku: z.string(), qty: z.number().int().positive() })),
  }),
  action: "invoice.create",            // the same Cedar action as the UI button
  confirm: false,
  async run({ input, billing }) {
    return billing.createInvoice(input.customerId, input.items);
  },
});
```

| Concern | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Registration | Every file under `functions/tools/` plus tools declared by installed modules (`[[tools]]` in `module.toml`) appear in `tools/list` at `GET /mcp`. The `billing` module ships `create_invoice`, `get_subscription`; `storage` ships `upload_file`; `org` ships `invite_member`; and so on |
| Identity | End users' agents authenticate through OAuth 2.1 provided by the `auth` module (Renox acts as the authorization server). The token carries the user and scopes, so "Alice's agent" can only do what Alice can |
| Authorization | Each tool declares an `action`; Cedar evaluates it with the token's user as principal, exactly like a UI action. No bypass path |
| Resources | Declared public views and read models can be exposed as read-only MCP resources (`resource://billing/invoices/{id}`), filtered by the same policies |
| Limits | Rate limit per token, timeout per tool call, output size cap, and per-call metering billed to the tenant |
| Confirmation | Tools marked `confirm: true` (payments, refunds, deletes) return a preview; the agent must send a confirmation token to execute |
| Discovery | `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and tool descriptions are served so general-purpose agents can find and connect to the app |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP on `/mcp`; SSE for server-initiated notifications (job finished, new message) |

Tool inputs are validated by the declared schema before `run`; outputs are serialized with a size cap and labeled as application data.

Status: served by the cell since #285 (`crates/renox-cell/src/mcp/`, README "App MCP"); resources and server-initiated SSE are not served yet.

## 3. In-app agents: tenant code calling models

```ts
const reply = await ctx.ai.chat({
  model: "claude-sonnet-5-5",
  system: "You are the support assistant for this shop.",
  messages,
  tools: [lookupOrder],        // local tools run in the same isolate under the same authz
  maxTokens: 800,
});
```

| Concern | Design |
| --- | --- |
| Outbound access | Through the `fetch` op with the provider host in the allowlist (`api.anthropic.com`, `api.openai.com`, or a local endpoint); API keys in secrets |
| Platform AI gateway (optional) | `ctx.ai` can route through a Renox-managed gateway that holds shared provider keys, meters tokens, enforces per-tenant spend limits, and caches identical requests. Small tenants need no provider account |
| Long-running agent loops | Run as durable jobs (outbox), not inside an HTTP request; progress streamed to the UI via SSE; resumable after restarts |
| Embeddings and semantic search | `sqlite-vec` in the tenant file; the `search` module adds a semantic mode |
| Limits | Tokens per request and per month count toward the tenant quota; wall-clock limits apply per tool call; the watchdog applies to local tool execution |
| Model choice | Default to the latest Claude models; provider is configurable per tenant |

## 4. Agent-friendly repository and CLI

- Every CLI command supports `--json` and `--yes` (non-interactive) and emits structured errors with `file:line`.
- `renox skill` generates skill files for popular agents (`.claude/skills/renox/SKILL.md`, Cursor rules, Codex instructions) containing the routing, template, module, and MCP tool conventions for the current project.
- `renox dev` exposes the error overlay through `dev_errors`, so an agent sees what a human sees in the browser.
- `AGENTS.md` and `docs/` in this repository are the canonical instructions for agents working on the platform itself.

## 5. Agent-specific security

| Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- |
| Prompt injection through data (a product name containing "ignore previous instructions") | Tool results from the database, logs, and user content are labeled `untrusted: true` in the MCP payload; SDK documentation requires agents to treat them as data; no tool executes free text as a command |
| Over-privileged agents | Per-tool scopes, read-only defaults, two-step confirmation for destructive tools, short-lived tokens, per-app grants |
| Secret leakage | Secrets are never serialized through MCP; logs and errors are redacted before leaving the cell |
| Quota exhaustion by runaway agents | Rate limits and metering per token; alerts to the tenant owner; automatic token suspension on anomalies |
| Attribution | Audit log distinguishes human and agent actors with client name and model; tenants can list and revoke agent tokens in the dashboard |
| Data exfiltration via tools | Output size caps; resources are policy-filtered; `db_export` requires a dedicated scope |

## 6. Build phases

| Part | Phase | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local `renox mcp` (dev_status, dev_errors, run_check, run_tests, docs resources) | F2–F3 | Cheap, and immediately speeds up our own agent-assisted development of Renox |
| Remote control-plane MCP with OAuth and scopes | F3–F4 | Needs the control plane and the token system |
| App MCP (`functions/tools/`, module tools, `/mcp` per app) | F5 | Needs Cedar and the `auth` module acting as OAuth server |
| `ctx.ai`, AI gateway, durable agent jobs | F7 | Needs mature metering and billing |

Components are tracked as P21 (platform MCP) and P22 (app MCP + `ctx.ai`) in `18-build-plan.md`.

---

Source: cli/README.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/cli/README.md)

# renox CLI (v0, F3)

One CLI for the tenant dev loop and deploys (`docs/12-developer-experience.md`, P11): `new`, `build`, `dev`, `check`, `mcp` (P21), and against the control plane `login`, `tokens`, `deploy`, `logs`, `secrets`, `db`. Bun, no runtime dependencies (the TOML parser, transpiler, bundler, and file watcher are Bun's own; the JSON Schema checks use `src/lib/schema.ts` against `docs/contracts/schemas`).

```
bun cli/src/main.ts <command>        # from the repository
bun run --cwd cli compile            # single binary: cli/dist/renox
bun test --cwd cli                   # tests; the dev end-to-end test needs RENOX_WORKER_PATH
```

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | ok | `renox check` with warnings only; `renox`, `renox help` |
| `1` | user error | unknown command or flag, bad `--port`, an invalid app name or a non-empty folder for `renox new`, no `renox.toml` (not in an app folder) |
| `2` | validation error | invalid TOML, an unknown key, a bad time zone or value in `renox.toml`; a bad route file name, two files for one route, paths that differ only in case; a TypeScript syntax or bundling error; any `renox check` error |
| `3` | environment error | no `renox-worker` binary (`RENOX_WORKER_PATH` unset and none downloaded, or pointing to nothing); the worker exits during startup or keeps exiting under `renox dev`; the port is in use |
| `130` | interrupted | Ctrl-C (SIGINT); `renox dev` stops the worker first |

Commands that call the control plane (`deploy`, `logs`, `secrets`, `db`, `tokens`, `login`) map the API's answer onto the same codes: not signed in, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 → `1` (with the API's code, message and `details`); 422 `RENOX_DEPLOY_REJECTED` and `RENOX_ACTIVATION_FAILED` → `2` (the artifact or its migrations, cell or probe are wrong); 5xx, 429 and an unreachable API → `3` (after the retries below). A command never prints a token or a secret value.

Every error is one message: `renox <command>: <file>:<line>:<col>: <what is wrong>`, then `hint: <what to do>` when there is something to do (`src/errors.ts`). `renox check` prints each problem as `<file>:<line>  error  <message>`. A TypeScript syntax error carries the transpiler's line and column, relative to the app folder. A `renox.toml` problem carries the line of the key; for a TOML syntax error, the line where parsing first fails. An unknown key comes with the closest valid key ("did you mean"). The messages are snapshotted in `tests/negative/__snapshots__/`.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `renox new <name> [--template blank\|hello]` | Creates `<name>/` with `renox.toml`, `package.json` (depends on `renox` at this CLI's own version, `^<cli version>`: the SDK is published at the same version, #376), `tsconfig.json`, `.gitignore`, the agent files `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcp.json` (the app model and rules in short, and `renox mcp --project .` registered for Claude Code and Cursor, #377; `cli/templates/`), and the template's files (`cli/templates/<template>/`; `hello` mirrors `examples/hello`, `blank` has `GET /api/health`). Refuses a non-empty folder |
| `renox build [--out <dir>]` | Builds the artifact (`docs/contracts/artifact.md`, version 1) into `.renox/artifact/<hash>/` (or `<dir>/<hash>/`). Leaves forbidden files out of `public/` and fails on a secret in what it ships (step 5 and the secret scan below). Prints the hash. An app with templates needs the `renox-worker` binary (see "Templates") |
| `renox dev [--port 8787]` | Builds, starts the prebuilt `renox-worker` on the app, serves it on `http://localhost:<port>`, rebuilds on every change and switches the worker to the new artifact. WebSocket and SSE routes are proxied unbuffered (below, "Realtime, tools and jobs") |
| `renox dev --worker <path>` | Runs another `renox-worker` binary: it must have the pinned release's sha256 or carry a sigstore signature (`<path>.sigstore.json`) and the release's provenance bundle beside it that `cosign` verifies; otherwise `RENOX_CLI_WORKER_UNVERIFIED`, exit code 3 (#129) |
| `renox check [--secrets] [--security] [--json] [--strict]` | Validates `renox.toml`, the modules and `renox.lock` (MF rules), route conflicts, templates, `[security]`, and the manifest (by building in memory), lints the sources, and scans for secrets. `--secrets` runs only the secret scan; `--security` also prints the effective response headers, CORS, and rate-limit buckets per route (#47). Exit code 2 on any error |
| `renox add <module> [--version <range>] [--source …] [--mount <path>] [--yes]` | Installs a module after showing and approving its permissions; writes `renox.toml` and `renox.lock` (below) |
| `renox remove <module>` | Uninstalls a module; its tables stay |
| `renox test [pattern...] [--seed <file.sql>]... [-u]` | Runs the policy test cases of `policies/tests/*.json`, then `tests/*.test.ts` with `renox/test` on the worker, a fresh tenant file per test file (below) |
| `renox authz explain --user <id> --action <a> [--resource <type:id>] [--role <r>]... [--db <file>] [--json]` | Why the app's policies allow or deny one request: the decision, the deciding policies with their text, evaluation errors. Roles and the resource's declared attributes come from the dev tenant file (below, "Authorization") |
| `renox dev --jobs` | Also runs the app's and modules' scheduled jobs (`jobs/*.ts`, ops.md section 20) and prints `jobs: <job> tick <time>` lines; without it, only queued runs (`ctx.jobs.enqueue`) run |
| `renox jobs list [--state scheduled\|queued\|running\|dead] [--json]` | The dev app's jobs from `.renox/data/dev/app.db`: next and last runs, the queue, running runs, dead runs with their last error; never a payload (#297) |
| `renox jobs run <name> [--module <m>]` | A tick of the scheduled job now (coalescing into its waiting run, as the scheduler does); `renox dev` runs it within a second |
| `renox jobs retry <id>` | A dead run back in the queue with its attempts reset |
| `renox migrate [--db <file>]` | Builds, then runs the artifact's migration plan (installed modules in lock order, then the app's) on the dev tenant file `.renox/data/dev/app.db` through `renox-worker migrate` (below) |
| `renox deploy [--json]` | Builds, uploads, validates and activates the app of `renox.toml` against the control plane (below) |
| `renox deploy --rollback [<hash>] [--app <name>] [--json]` | Switches the app back to the previous deployment, or to the superseded one named by a hash or a unique prefix of at least 6 characters |
| `renox logs [--follow] [--since <t>] [--source all\|server\|client] [--deployment <hash>] [--app <name>] [--json]` | The app's log lines; `--follow` keeps streaming |
| `renox secrets set <NAME> \| list \| rm <NAME> [--app <name>]` | App secrets; `set` reads the value from stdin |
